name: Maine
rateNote: 18-month redemption via tax lien mortgage — municipal process
keyNotes: Tax lien mortgage system — municipality holds lien, not sold directly to investors in most cases
After 18 months unredeemed, municipality forecloses and may sell property
PL 2025, c. 351 update — verify current municipal procedures
Retail investor access is limited — primarily municipal sales of foreclosed properties

pendingLegislation.summary: 2025 update to Maine tax lien mortgage procedures. Verify current municipal requirements before transacting.

summary: Maine municipalities hold tax liens. After 18 months, municipality takes title and can auction. No centralized state system. Statute: MRSA Title 36 §942.
typeWhy: Maine municipalities hold tax liens — the municipality itself purchases the lien, and after 18 months of non-redemption, the municipality takes title and can auction the property. MRSA Title 36 §942.
rateWhy: Maine sets the interest rate on municipal tax liens at 8% per annum by statute. This is a fixed rate applied uniformly. MRSA Title 36 §942.
notBeginnerReason: Municipal-level only, sporadic auctions, very low volume. Not a viable primary market.
beginnerTip: Portland and Bangor have the most consistent municipal auction activity. For rural towns, call the town office directly — many don't advertise sales publicly.
risks: Municipalities conduct sales infrequently and irregularly
No centralized platform — requires monitoring individual town tax collectors
ddExtra: Contact the municipal tax collector at least 6 months before any expected sale
Confirm the municipality plans to auction rather than negotiate or hold the property
Check for conservation easements or deed restrictions before bidding

steps: Identify your target municipality at maine.gov/revenue/propertytax
Contact the municipal tax collector at least 6 months before any expected auction
Request the delinquent property list and auction schedule
Register per municipality instructions — most are in-person

tylerCompliance.summary: Status pending — monitoring for legislative action.
tylerCompliance.details: This state compliance with Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) is currently being monitored. Aurigen tracks legislative updates, pending bills, and court decisions that affect tax sale surplus requirements. Check back for updates.

rules.statute: MRS Title 36, §942 (Lien Certificate) + §943 (Tax Lien Mortgage) + §943-C (Sale of Foreclosed Property)
rules.structure: 493+ municipalities run independent tax lien processes. No county-level auction. Each town/city manages its own tax-acquired property.

process.step1: Taxes delinquent → tax collector makes demand for payment + notice
process.step2: Tax collector files tax lien certificate in county Registry of Deeds — creates 'tax lien mortgage' on property
process.step3: Municipality sends certified mail copy to record owner and all mortgage holders
process.step4: 30–45 days before 18-month deadline: treasurer sends certified mail notice of impending foreclosure with exact date
process.step5: 18 months from lien filing: AUTOMATIC FORECLOSURE — municipality owns property without court order
process.step6: Municipality sells under §943-C: must list with licensed RE broker at highest reasonable price. At least 12 months to sell.

auction.platform: Municipality-run — listed with licensed ME real estate broker (§943-C requirement)
auction.notice: Former owner must receive advance notice of intent to sell. May require former owner to execute QC deed conveying interest before receiving excess proceeds.
auction.statute: MRS §943-C (as amended by PL 2024, enacted per PL 2023, c.640 + St.2024)

otc.name: N/A — Maine tax-acquired property sold via RE broker under §943-C
otc.note: Contact individual municipalities directly for tax-acquired property listings

subTax.name: N/A — Maine lien stays with municipality unless assigned (bulk sale option)

taxTitleAssignment.name: Tax Title Assignment (MGL c.60 §52 equivalent)
taxTitleAssignment.statute: MRS §943 — municipality may assign tax lien mortgage to private party
taxTitleAssignment.note: Bulk sale option: municipality may assign right to collect tax obligation to private investor per §943. Less common than municipal retention.

redemption.period: 18 months from date tax lien certificate filed in Registry of Deeds
redemption.lateNoticeException: If required notices not sent timely — mortgagee/owner may redeem within 3 months of receiving actual knowledge of lien recording
redemption.probateExtension: Probate court may extend up to 60 days following final allowance/disallowance of will
redemption.interestRate: Municipality-set. Maximum: prime rate (WSJ first business day of year) + 3 percentage points, rounded up to nearest whole number. No statewide fixed rate.
redemption.costToRedeem: All taxes + interest + recording fees + $13 + certified mail fees

deedPath.name: Automatic Foreclosure — Municipality Owns (no court required)
deedPath.effect: At 18 months from lien recording — municipality automatically owns property. Tax lien mortgage is prima facie evidence of title regularity.
deedPath.postForeclosure: Municipality must sell via licensed RE broker per §943-C. Must send former owner pre-sale notice.
deedPath.formerOwnerPostDeed: Former owner may execute QC deed and waive §946-B challenge right to receive excess proceeds. This enables marketable title.
deedPath.note: ⚡ PL 2024 amendment: post-sale notice of intent to distribute must be sent to former owners and all parties with recorded interests. Itemized accounting available on request. Within 10 days of distributing proceeds — municipality records notice at Registry.

surplus.name: Excess Sale Proceeds
surplus.definition: Sale proceeds minus: all delinquent taxes that would have accrued during municipal ownership + fees (advertising, mailing, recording, RE broker fees) + admin costs + attorney fees + utility charges
surplus.process: Notice mailed to former owner at last known address. If not located → published in local newspaper. If former owner fails to claim within 30 days of final published notice → transferred to state unclaimed property fund.
surplus.formerOwnerRequest: Former owner may request written accounting and itemization of deductions
surplus.waiver: Former owner who receives excess proceeds waives right to contest foreclosure under §946-B
surplus.note: Tyler v. Hennepin directly influenced ME §943-C overhaul in 2023/2024. Municipalities now MUST return surplus to former owners.

es.summary: Los municipios de Maine realizan gravámenes fiscales. Después de 18 meses, el municipio toma el título y puede subastar. Sin sistema estatal centralizado. Estatuto: MRSA Título 36 §942.
es.typeWhy: Maine es un estado de gravamen porque los municipios retienen gravámenes fiscales. Después de 18 meses sin redención, el municipio toma el título (MRSA Título 36 §942).
es.rateWhy: La tasa del 8% es relativamente baja entre los estados de gravamen. Refleja el volumen limitado y la naturaleza esporádica de las ventas municipales (MRSA Título 36 §942).
es.notBeginnerReason: Solo a nivel municipal, subastas esporádicas, volumen muy bajo. No es un mercado primario viable.
es.beginnerTip: Portland y Bangor tienen la actividad más consistente en ME. Para pueblos rurales, llame directamente a la oficina municipal — muchos no anuncian ventas públicamente.
risks: Los municipios realizan ventas con poca frecuencia e irregularmente
ddExtra: Contacte al recaudador municipal al menos 6 meses antes de cualquier venta esperada
Confirme que el municipio planea subastar en lugar de negociar o retener
Revise servidumbres de conservación o restricciones antes de pujar

steps: Identifique su municipio objetivo en maine.gov/revenue/propertytax
Contacte al recaudador de impuestos municipal al menos 6 meses antes
Solicite la lista de propiedades en mora y el calendario de subasta
Regístrese según instrucciones del municipio — la mayoría son en persona
